title: Missile Strikes Riyadh Airport Terminal, Wounding Many as Flights Divert
excerpt: Saturday's missile strike on a Riyadh airport terminal — the third attack in a week — wounded many, shut the airport and forced Gulf airlines to divert and cancel flights.
body:
• A missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, wounding many people, two regional officials told Reuters; more than a dozen ambulances rushed to the airport and travellers were evacuated from parts of the facility.
  • All flights to Riyadh were diverted or cancelled — Flightradar24 showed planes heading mainly to Jeddah — and Kuwait Airways, Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways suspended services as the airport urged passengers to check their flight status before leaving home.
  • The attack is the third on the airport in a week amid a Saudi-led offensive against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis; the Houthis claimed the earlier strikes but had not commented on Saturday's attack.
  • Flying to Saudi Arabia soon? Confirm your flight with your airline first — Indian carriers had already suspended some Riyadh services after the earlier strikes this week, and India's foreign ministry has advised nationals in Saudi Arabia to stay alert.

A missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, wounding many people and shutting down one of the Gulf's busiest aviation hubs, two regional officials told Reuters. Ambulances were seen rushing toward the airport and travellers were evacuated from parts of the facility after a loud blast rocked the Saudi capital in the afternoon.

One eyewitness told Reuters he saw an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside the airport. More than a dozen ambulances converged on the scene, according to an eyewitness and people briefed on the matter. A Riyadh resident told the Associated Press he heard at least two loud explosions.

Third strike in a week

Saturday's attack is the third on King Khalid International Airport in a week. The airport was hit twice earlier in the week, leaving four people dead — including three Saudi citizens, one of them a pilot, killed in Wednesday's strike — and badly damaging an aircraft. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those earlier attacks.

There was no immediate Houthi statement on Saturday's blast. The Saudi government-run Centre for International Communication did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and neither did the Saudi civil aviation authority. The strikes come as a Saudi-led coalition pursues a major military offensive against the Houthis in neighbouring Yemen. The group has declared Saudi airspace a zone of military operations and warned airliners to avoid it.

Flights grounded across the Gulf

Flight-tracking site Flightradar24 said all flights to Riyadh had been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point. The last commercial flight landed at 2:05 pm local time and the last departure was at 1:39 pm; inbound planes were diverted mainly to Jeddah.

Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights to and from the Saudi capital, citing the airport's closure because of the "security situation" there. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways cancelled multiple flights between their hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Earlier Houthi attacks on Thursday had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital — shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organisers said on Saturday the conferences would go ahead as planned.

Canada's embassy advised citizens to avoid all travel to the airport, noting "ongoing military activity."

Diaspora angle

Saudi Arabia hosts one of the largest Indian expatriate communities in the world, and the strikes land just as many families plan travel around the festival season. India's foreign ministry on October 8 advised Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia to stay alert after the earlier Houthi strikes, and Indian carriers had already suspended some Riyadh flights. Anyone with bookings to the kingdom this week should reconfirm with their airline — and Indian travellers currently in Saudi Arabia should keep the Indian embassy's emergency contacts handy.

What's next

Attention now turns to whether the Houthis claim Saturday's attack and whether Saudi Arabia responds with retaliation in Yemen. With energy and investment conferences on the calendar and airlines already extending cancellations into next week, the disruption could stretch well beyond a single day of violence. The trajectory of the Saudi-led offensive in Yemen will likely determine whether Riyadh's airport faces a fourth strike.
